title: What Makes a Relationship Work: Putting It All Together

sections.title: Five lessons, one reflection
sections.content: You now have the full toolkit for talking about relationships: reciprocal actions with egymás in its various cases (szeretjük egymást, segítenek egymásnak), the -kodik-family verbs of conflict and support (veszekedik, összevész valakivel, gondoskodik valakiről, ragaszkodik valakihez), and the concessive frame annak ellenére, hogy for holding two contrasting truths in one sentence. One more small piece rounds it out: is... is ("both... and"), used to list more than one quality or person at once.

sections.title: New: is... is ("both... and")
rows: Mind érzelmileg, mind gyakorlatilag támogatjuk egymást.
We support each other both emotionally and practically.
Anna is, Péter is mindig számíthat rám.
Both Anna and Péter can always count on me.

items.spanish: Annak ellenére, hogy néha összeveszünk, mindig kibékülünk, és utána jobban megértjük egymást.
items.english: Even though we sometimes fall out, we always make up, and afterward we understand each other even better.

items.spanish: A jó kapcsolat titka, hogy gondoskodunk egymásról, annak ellenére, hogy néha nehéz.
items.english: The secret of a good relationship is that we take care of each other, despite the fact that it's sometimes hard.

items.spanish: Az igazi barátság az, amikor ragaszkodunk egymáshoz, akkor is, ha nem értünk mindenben egyet.
items.english: True friendship is when we stay attached to each other, even when we don't agree on everything.

sections.content: When you're combining several of these pieces in one sentence, build it clause by clause: settle the concession (annak ellenére, hogy...) first, then the main statement with its own egymás case and its own verb government. Trying to force one case ending to serve two different verbs is the most common mistake at this level.
